8.2. Conservation and Incompressibility🔗

Particle paths and material derivatives turn local conservation of mass and momentum into the Eulerian equations.

8.2.1. From Conservation Laws to Incompressible Flow🔗

8.2.1.1. From Transport to Fluid Motion🔗

The simplest evolution in the hierarchy is a scalar carried by a prescribed velocity. The transport equation

\partial_t\theta+u\cdot\nabla\theta=0

says that \theta is constant along particle paths. The velocity is known, so the equation is linear in the transported scalar. The characteristic chain rule is the scalar counterpart of the particle-path chain rule.

In one space dimension, allowing the transported quantity to determine its own speed gives inviscid Burgers, \partial_tu+u\,\partial_xu=0. Characteristics can intersect, smooth solutions can form shocks, and weak solutions then require an entropy condition. Incompressible Euler retains the self-transport mechanism, but the velocity is vector-valued and pressure enforces the divergence-free constraint.

A fluid is described in Eulerian variables by fields attached to positions in space: density \rho(t,x), velocity u(t,x), and pressure p(t,x). A particle released at a follows a trajectory X(t,a) satisfying

\frac{d}{dt}X(t,a)=u(t,X(t,a)).

If a scalar or vector field v is observed along that particle path, the chain rule gives

\frac{d}{dt}v(t,X(t,a)) =\partial_t v+(u\mathbin\cdot\nabla)v.

This is the material derivative. For prescribed u it is linear in the transported field v. The fluid nonlinearity appears when v=u, because the unknown velocity then transports itself.

A particle path is represented by the local identity

X'(t)=u(t,X(t)).

The pointwise predicate is useful when only a local calculation is needed. Its setwise form requires the same identity throughout a time interval.

✓L∃∀N

If X is a particle path, the associated spacetime curve t\mapsto(t,X(t)) has velocity (1,u(t,X(t))). Therefore every differentiable spacetime field v satisfies

\frac{d}{dt}v(t,X(t)) =Dv(t,X(t))[1,u(t,X(t))].

For scalar v, expanding the Fréchet derivative gives the checked identity

\frac{d}{dt}v(t,X(t)) =\partial_t v(t,X(t)) +\sum_{j=1}^n u_j(t,X(t))\,\partial_jv(t,X(t)).

Proof for Theorem 8.6
uses 0

Write the spacetime trajectory as the sum of its time coordinate and the zero-time embedding of X. Their derivatives are respectively the time basis vector and the embedded spatial velocity. The ordinary Fréchet chain rule gives the directional derivative, and expansion in the Euclidean coordinate basis separates its time coordinate from the spatial sum.

8.2.1.2. Mass and incompressibility🔗

Conservation of mass is the continuity equation

\partial_t\rho+\nabla\mathbin\cdot(\rho u)=0.

The mass flux is \rho u, and the continuity residual is

R_\rho=\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho u).

The material derivative of density is D_t^u\rho=\partial_t\rho+u\cdot\nabla\rho.

Proof for Theorem 8.8
uses 0

Apply the product rule to each component \partial_j(\rho u_j), sum over the spatial coordinates, and collect the terms u_j\partial_j\rho. The remaining sum is \rho\sum_j\partial_ju_j.

✓L∃∀N

If \rho=\rho_0 is constant, then

R_\rho=\rho_0\,\nabla\cdot u.

Every divergence-free flow therefore conserves constant density. When \rho_0\ne0, the continuity equation and incompressibility are equivalent.

Proof for Theorem 8.9
uses 0

The time derivative of a constant vanishes, and constant scalar multiplication passes through every spatial partial derivative. Thus the continuity residual is \rho_0 times the divergence. If \rho_0 is nonzero, their product vanishes exactly when the divergence vanishes.

Incompressibility, \nabla\cdot u=0, says that an infinitesimal fluid volume neither expands nor contracts.

Definition 8.11

✓L∃∀N

Write spacetime as \mathbb R^{n+1}, with coordinate zero reserved for time. The material derivative is

(D_t^u v)_i =\partial_t v_i+\sum_{j=1}^n u_j\partial_jv_i,

and incompressibility sums only the spatial derivatives. The global condition requires this sum to vanish everywhere; its pointwise form imposes the same identity at one spacetime point.

An incompressible solution pairs an equation-specific momentum predicate with incompressibility and initial data. A residual solution requires only those equations; a classical solution adds the regularity that makes the totalized derivatives analytic derivatives and the assigned initial value a one-sided trace. Global solutions restrict canonically to any positive finite horizon. Euler and Navier–Stokes are both instances of these definitions.

8.2.1.3. Momentum and stress🔗

Incompressibility allows substantial deformation. For the planar velocity u(x,y)=(ax,-ay), the divergence is a-a=0, while particles follow (x(t),y(t))=(e^{at}x(0),e^{-at}y(0)). A small rectangle stretches in one direction and contracts in the other; the area factor is e^{at}e^{-at}=1. This example helps us read \nabla\cdot u=0: it controls volume change, not the size of the velocity or the amount of stretching.

Newton's law for a continuum reads

\rho D_tu=\nabla\mathbin\cdot\sigma+\rho f,

where \sigma is the Cauchy stress tensor and f is an external force per unit mass. For an incompressible Newtonian fluid with constant density, the stress splits into pressure and viscosity:

\sigma=-pI+2\mu D(u),\qquad D(u)=\frac12\bigl(\nabla u+\nabla u^{\mathsf T}\bigr).

The spatial velocity gradient has components (\nabla u)_{ij}=\partial_j u_i. Its symmetric part is the strain rate

D_{ij}(u)=\frac{\partial_j u_i+\partial_i u_j}{2},

and the Newtonian constitutive law is

\sigma_{ij}=-p\,\delta_{ij}+2\mu D_{ij}(u).

The velocity gradient splits into its symmetric and antisymmetric parts:

\partial_j u_i=D_{ij}(u)+\frac12\Omega_{ij}(u), \qquad D_{ji}(u)=D_{ij}(u).

Here \Omega_{ij}(u)=\partial_j u_i-\partial_i u_j is twice the antisymmetric part of the velocity gradient, developed as vorticity in the Euler section.

Proof for Theorem 8.12
uses 0

Add and subtract \partial_i u_j. Half of their sum is the strain rate, and half of their difference is \Omega_{ij}/2, the antisymmetric part. Exchanging the two indices leaves the sum unchanged.

To see why the symmetric part measures strain, let h be an infinitesimal separation between two particles. Along a smooth trajectory its linearized evolution is h'=(\nabla u)h, so

\frac{d}{dt}|h|^2=2h\cdot(\nabla u)h=2h\cdot D(u)h.

An antisymmetric matrix contributes zero to this quadratic form. It can rotate the separation without changing its length. For the stretching flow u=(ax,-ay), D(u)=\operatorname{diag}(a,-a); for solid rotation, D(u)=0 even though the velocity and vorticity are nonzero.

The diagonal of D(u) carries the volumetric information: for incompressible flow the pressure is the only part of the stress that survives on the trace.

The strain trace is the divergence:

\operatorname{tr}D(u)=\sum_i\partial_i u_i=\nabla\cdot u.

Consequently, incompressible strain is trace free. The Newtonian stress is symmetric because both the pressure tensor and D(u) are symmetric.

Proof for Theorem 8.13
uses 0

On the diagonal, D_{ii}=(\partial_i u_i+\partial_i u_i)/2=\partial_i u_i. Summing gives the divergence, which vanishes under incompressibility. Symmetry of the stress follows componentwise from \delta_{ij}=\delta_{ji} and D_{ij}=D_{ji}.

Newton's law involves the stress only through \nabla\cdot\sigma. Differentiating the constitutive law componentwise turns the pressure part into -\nabla p and the strain part into a Laplacian plus a gradient of the divergence, the latter being the same trace that incompressibility has just removed.

Theorem 8.15
Loading preview
Reverse dependency preview content is loaded from the rendered-fragment cache.
✓L∃∀N

For constant dynamic viscosity \mu, taking the spatial divergence of the Newtonian constitutive law gives

(\nabla\cdot\sigma)_i =-\partial_i p+\mu\Delta u_i+\mu\,\partial_i(\nabla\cdot u).

For a divergence-free velocity, the final term vanishes and therefore

\nabla\cdot\sigma=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u.

The formal statement assumes differentiability of pressure and componentwise C^2 regularity of velocity at the point, so that mixed spatial derivatives commute. Its incompressible conclusion assumes divergence-freeness on the whole field, since the gradient of the divergence must vanish at the point.

Proof for Theorem 8.14
uses 0

Differentiate \sigma_{ij}=-p\delta_{ij}+\mu(\partial_j u_i+\partial_i u_j) with respect to x_j and sum over j. The pressure terms select -\partial_i p; the first viscous sum is \mu\Delta u_i. Commuting the mixed derivatives in the second viscous sum gives \mu\partial_i\sum_j\partial_j u_j. This is \mu\partial_i(\nabla\cdot u), which is zero when the divergence vanishes identically.

Substituting the reduced stress divergence into \rho D_tu=\nabla\cdot\sigma+\rho f at unit density is all that separates the Cauchy momentum balance from the Navier–Stokes equation.

used by 0✓L∃∀N

At unit density, the Cauchy momentum residual is

R_C=D_t^u u-\nabla\cdot\sigma-f.

For a divergence-free Newtonian velocity field with the stated differentiability, it is exactly the Navier–Stokes residual:

R_C =D_t^u u+\nabla p-\mu\Delta u-f =R_{NS}.

Thus the Cauchy momentum balance and the reduced Navier–Stokes equation are the same pointwise equation under these hypotheses.

  (p : ℝ^(n + 1) → ℝ)
  (u f : ℝ^(n + 1) → ℝ^n)
  (x : ℝ^(n + 1)) : ℝ^n

    Unit-density Cauchy momentum residual Dₜu - div σ - f for Newtonian stress.

Proof for Theorem 8.15
uses 0

Substitute \nabla\cdot\sigma=-\nabla p+\mu\Delta u into D_t^u u-\nabla\cdot\sigma-f. Distributing the minus sign gives D_t^u u+\nabla p-\mu\Delta u-f, component by component.

For constant density \rho_0>0, divide the momentum equation by \rho_0, replace pressure by p/\rho_0, and set \nu=\mu/\rho_0. Together with \nabla\cdot u=0, this gives

\partial_tu+(u\mathbin\cdot\nabla)u+\nabla p =\nu\Delta u+f.

The equation must be paired with a spatial domain and boundary conditions. On a rigid wall, impermeability requires u\cdot n=0; the viscous no-slip condition strengthens this to u=0. Whole-space problems instead prescribe decay or integrability at infinity, while periodic problems identify opposite faces of a box. These choices affect pressure recovery, energy identities, and the meaning of a weak solution.

The operators distinguish \partial_tu, (u\cdot\nabla_x)v, \nu\Delta_xu, and \nabla_xp. Every spatial operator uses only coordinates 1,\ldots,n; coordinate zero remains time. This matters because the ambient fields live on spacetime, where an unqualified Laplacian would also differentiate twice in time.

Proof for Theorem 8.17
uses 0

Evaluate both sides in a velocity component. The definitions have the same time partial and the same finite sum of spatial directional derivatives, so the componentwise equality is immediate.

✓L∃∀N

On a finite horizon [0,T], a momentum test field is a smooth compactly supported spacetime vector field \varphi satisfying \varphi(T,x)=0. It may be nonzero at t=0, which exposes the initial boundary term after integration by parts. The velocity and initial pairings are

\langle u(t),\psi\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u(t,x)\cdot\psi(x)\,dx, \qquad \langle u_0,\psi\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_0(x)\cdot\psi(x)\,dx.

These are shared test data and pairings; the Euler and Navier–Stokes weak formulations supply their own momentum integrands.
